episodes.209936: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
episodes.210077: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.
episodes.210213: A stationary front stalled out across Ohio and Indiana, sparking showers and thunderstorms along the boundary. Some of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in instances of flash flooding.
episodes.210214: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, sparking thunderstorms in a moist airmass. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.210265: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced localized wind damage over Hardy County, WV.
episodes.210284: Severe thunderstorms with large hail fell across portions of southwest Missouri during the morning of March 4th. Additional thunderstorms with large hail fell across southern Missouri during the evening of March 4th. The two rounds of thunderstorms produced a swatch of 2-4 inches of rainfall from Cassville to Springfield to Salem. This rainfall caused localized flooding.
episodes.210812: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
episodes.210973: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 4th, ahead of a cold front moving into the region. The thunderstorms continued to affect the area through the early morning hours of the 5th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to golf ball size.
episodes.210997: On the night of the 3rd and 4th of March, an upper level system moved in to the combined Panhandles sparking a line of thunderstorms running southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle. The southern most storm developed into a severe storm that dropped hail up to 2 in diameter across Potter and Randall County.  On the evening of the 5th of March increase moisture advection in the southeastern Panhandles provided instability for severe thunderstorms. This time in the southeastern Panhandles. One of these storms dropped hail up to 1.7 in Collingsworth County.
episodes.211257: Approximately 24 hours of near constant rainfall produced 2 to 5 inches of rain in southeast Missouri. This amount of rainfall caused Flat Creek to rise above its banks where it spilled into a nearby neighborhood. Evacuations were required, but no injuries or fatalities were reported.
episodes.211265: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, prompting showers and thunderstorms in a warm and moist airmass. Some storms produced locally heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding and high water.
episodes.211830: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed ahead of cold front extending from North Texas into Southeast Oklahoma during the evening of March 4th. Storm organization and mid-level rotation was noted with individual cells in the vicinity of the cold front as it shifted east along the Red River. Effective shear of 30-40 knots and MLCAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg was sufficient to support occasional supercells across the region, with an increasing coverage of storms in response to an associated mid-level shortwave trough ejecting eastward and coupled with a modest strengthening of the low-level jet. One supercell thunderstorm in particular resulted in localized damaging wind gusts in the Sherwood community east of U.S. Highway 259 in McCurtain County Oklahoma, snapping a few pine trees in this area.
episodes.212440: An outflow boundary from a collapsed thunderstorm moved west over Gulf of America waters north of Big Pine Key, producing isolated gale-force wind gusts.
